description:
In your home, wash bedding in hot water that is at least 130 F to kill dust mites and remove allergens. This is a born-as guide to house dust mites in a house: the bed, what they eat, heat and humidity, the eggs, a wash at least 130 F, the fact they never really leave, what the allergens can do, and what actually helps. Meatball lives all eight from the couch, with his dog, Noodle, as the stand-in and his cat, Sauce, as everybody else.

Checked facts in this video:
- Lead is the North American house dust mite (Dermatophagoides farinae). There are two common species in the United States: the North American house dust mite and the European house dust mite (D. pteronyssinus) (University of Kentucky ENTFACT-646). Life-cycle figures later on that page are for house dust mites generally, not a farinae-only count. This video does not mix in Demodex or any other mite.
- House dust mite adults are about 0.5 mm long; immatures are even smaller. They generally are visible only with a microscope. They are globular, clear to creamy white, with hairs on their legs and body (University of Kentucky). A thin University of Maine page says they measure, on average, just 16 hundredths of an inch; that length is not used and is not spoken (D5).
- Their primary food is skin scales, or dander, contained in house dust. People and pets regularly shed small flakes of skin as the skin continually renews itself. Since the greatest fallout occurs in areas of human and pet activity, the mites tend to be most numerous in beds, overstuffed sofas and chairs, and adjacent carpeted areas (University of Kentucky). Keep "tend to be most numerous." Beds are one of several sites. This is not "they only live in your bed."
- Relative humidity also tends to be higher in these areas, because people perspire and exhale water vapor where they sleep and lounge. Mattresses, sofas, carpet, and other soft furnishings trap and accumulate dust, dander, and moisture, making them ideal microhabitats for mite development (University of Kentucky).
- Dust mites can live in bedding, mattresses, upholstered furniture, carpets and curtains (American Lung Association). A different official page (EPA) adds pillows, clothes, stuffed toys, fabric, and fabric-covered items, and says dust mites are tiny bugs that are too small to see. Those lists are not merged into one official list.
- House dust mites are typically found on the floors, mattresses, rugs, or infesting dried stored products, where they feed on micro molds that develop on skin scales and foods (University of Kentucky). Keep the "micro molds that develop on skin scales and foods" hedge. They do not "eat you." A different official page (National Jewish Health) calls them microscopic animals that feed on human skin scales, and live in bedding, carpets, stuffed furniture, old clothing and stuffed toys.
- House dust mites are not parasitic, and they are not capable of biting or stinging humans. Their significance as pests is due to the powerful allergens contained in the mites, their cast skins, fecal material and secretions (University of Kentucky). A different official page (American Lung Association) says they are not parasites that bite, sting, or burrow into our bodies. People who are allergic are reacting to inhaling proteins in dust that comes from dust mite feces, urine, or decaying bodies. This video does not call them insects. If "insect-like" appears on a page, it is not upgraded to "insects."
- Optimum conditions for growth and development are around 75 to 80 degrees Fahrenheit, and 70 to 80 percent relative humidity. House dust mites absorb and lose moisture through their skin, and are very vulnerable to dehydration. The mites tend to be most numerous in warm homes with high humidity (University of Kentucky). Keep "around" and "optimum."
- Some species of house dust mites require a high relative humidity ranging from 70 to 80 percent, whereas others can survive in lower levels, between 50 and 60 percent. Dust mites cannot survive well at relative humidities below 50 percent. The same page also says house dust mites have a difficult time surviving when the relative humidity is below 50 percent (University of Kentucky). Keep "cannot survive well" / "difficult time," not "all die at 50 percent." The 50 to 60 percent survival line is why 50 percent is a hedge, not a hard kill switch.
- Although mite populations tend to be low in dry climates, most homes throughout the United States are capable of supporting dust mites (University of Kentucky). A different official page (American Lung Association) says dust mites do not drink water; instead, they absorb moisture from the air. When indoor air is very dry, dust mites cannot survive. "Very dry" is not given as a percentage on that page; this video does not invent one.
- Mayo Clinic: keep humidity low; maintain a relative humidity below 50 percent in your home. American Lung Association: keep your home below 50 percent humidity. Those action lines stay consistent with "cannot survive well" if "well" stays. A different official page (National Jewish Health) says dust mites don't survive when the humidity is below 50 percent, and that humidity should be below 40 percent, with 40 to 50 percent "marginal" and 50 to 60 percent "can be bothersome." That wording is stronger. It is not spoken in this video, is not blended with "cannot survive well," and is not averaged into one unofficial target (D2).
- House dust mites go through five major life stages: egg, larva, protonymph, tritonymph, and adult. Between life stages the mites molt, shedding their outer skin. When temperature and humidity are optimum, development from egg to adult takes about one month (University of Kentucky). Keep the optimum condition. Adults live approximately 1 to 2 months, and the females lay about 50 eggs (University of Kentucky). Keep "approximately," "about," and "house dust mites generally." Do not add "in your bed" to the egg-count sentence. That merge is cut (M1).
- Every home has dust mites (EPA). A different official page says dust mites are common and can be found in almost every home (American Lung Association). Those are related, not identical, and are not spoken as one sentence (D4). About 4 out of 5 homes in the United States have dust mite allergens in at least one bed (American Lung Association). Keep "about," "allergens," and "at least one bed." This is not "80 percent of beds are infested."
- It is not uncommon to find thousands of mites in a single gram of house dust (a gram is about the weight of a paperclip). An infested mattress can contain millions of dust mites (University of Kentucky). Keep "not uncommon," "thousands," "an infested mattress," and "can contain millions." Not every mattress.
- Mayo Clinic: wash all sheets, blankets, pillowcases and bedcovers in hot water that is at least 130 F (54.4 C) to kill dust mites and remove allergens. Keep "at least." This is the pitch-locked wash. If bedding can't be washed hot, put the items in the dryer for at least 15 minutes at a temperature above 130 F (54.4 C) to kill the mites. Then wash and dry the bedding to remove allergens. Killing mites and removing allergens are separate steps. This is not a 20-minute dryer cycle (M2). Freezing items for 24 hours if they can't be washed also can kill dust mites. But this won't remove the allergens.
- Wash-temperature disagreement (D1): a different official page (American Lung Association) says wash bedding in hot water (at least 120 degrees F) once a week to kill and wash away dust mites, with the same 120 F line for stuffed animals. That is not the same as at least 130, and the two are not averaged. University of Kentucky says use only washable bed spreads, sheets and blankets, and launder bedding weekly in hot water, with no degree on that page. EPA says wash bedding in hot water once a week, and dry completely, also with no degree on this live page. Do not hang 130 F on University of Kentucky or this EPA page. National Jewish Health says washing all bedding in hot (130 F) water weekly; that page supports 130, but it does not say "at least," and it does not give the dryer alternative. These are description-only except the American Lung Association line, which is spoken. Weekly cadence is spoken only with that line, not hung on the Mayo "at least 130 F" sentence, which does not say weekly.
- These heat numbers are for laundry, and for the dryer and freezer alternatives. They are not a way to heat the whole house, and they are not a thermostat or space-heater trick (W6). This video does not use heat numbers from any other pest, and it does not offer a folk killer or a "safe" amount of mites.
- House dust mites and their allergenic particles are present within homes year-round, but people tend to have fewer symptoms during the summer, perhaps because they spend more time outdoors (University of Kentucky). Keep "perhaps." Adults living approximately 1 to 2 months is not the same as they're gone in two months, and they do not disappear in summer.
- The allergenic proteins responsible for causing symptoms are contained within the mites themselves (alive or dead), their shed skins, and especially in their feces. Routine human activity such as housecleaning, walking or playing on carpeting, or making the bed, causes the tiny fecal particles to become airborne and inhaled (University of Kentucky). This is not a "making the bed is dangerous" scare line. Symptoms of a house dust mite allergy include stuffy or runny nose, sneezing, coughing or watery eyes. Inhalation of dust mite allergens by hypersensitive individuals can result in acute attacks of bronchial asthma, accompanied by wheezing and shortness of breath (University of Kentucky). Keep "hypersensitive individuals" and "can." The same page also says "perhaps even death"; that wording is not used as a hook and is not spoken in this video (W5).
- Asthma-share disagreement (D3): recent studies suggest that at least 45 percent of young people with asthma are allergic to house dust mites (University of Kentucky). Keep "recent studies suggest," "at least 45 percent," and "young people with asthma." No named study is on the page. A different official page (American Lung Association) says up to 85 percent of individuals with asthma have an allergic reaction to dust mites that make their asthma worse. Keep "up to 85 percent," "individuals with asthma," and "can" on that page's other asthma lines. Those are not the same claim, and the two are not averaged. Another official page (National Jewish Health) says almost everyone is exposed, but not everyone is sensitive, and that children allergic to dust mites are five times more likely to develop asthma. Keep "children allergic to dust mites" (already allergic). If droppings of dust mites are inhaled or come in contact with the skin, they may cause allergic symptoms and aggravate asthma and/or eczema (National Jewish Health). That droppings/eczema line is not spoken in this video; it is kept here. A different official page (EPA) says body parts and droppings from dust mites can trigger asthma in individuals with allergies to dust mites, and, as a separate line, exposure to dust mites can cause asthma in children who have not previously exhibited asthma symptoms. Keep "can," and do not merge the second EPA sentence into the five-times claim.
- If you think you have dust mite allergy, take steps to reduce house dust, mainly in your bedroom. That is not a diagnosis. Keep your bedroom clean, remove dust-collecting clutter, and wash bedding in hot water that is at least 130 F (Mayo Clinic). Encase mattress, box springs, and pillows in allergen-impermeable covers (University of Kentucky). A different official page (EPA) says use dust-proof covers on pillows and mattresses; that wording is not spoken in this video and is not treated as a second official list spoken as one sentence.
- Vacuuming and cleaning activities have not shown much benefit in reducing mite populations, or removing their allergenic materials. Routine, thorough vacuuming can, however, help to remove dust, dander, and a small percentage of mites. When vacuuming is performed, it's important to use a vacuum cleaner equipped with a HEPA filtration system, so that the microscopic allergens are retained within the vacuum bag (University of Kentucky). This is not "vacuuming is useless" and not "vacuuming wipes them out." EPA and National Jewish Health still recommend vacuuming as a step; this video does not invent a fight between pages.
- Although benzyl benzoate will kill dust mites, clinical trials are lacking that show much improvement in allergy symptoms. The same is true of products containing tannic acid (e.g., Allergy Control Solution), which are designed to denature dust mite allergens so that they no longer cause symptoms. Treatment of the premises with either of these chemicals should be considered only as a supplement to more important allergy-reducing measures, such as encasement of bedding and removal of dust-laden furnishings. ALWAYS READ AND FOLLOW LABEL DIRECTIONS FOR SAFE USE OF ANY PESTICIDE (University of Kentucky). The brand example is not spoken and is not an endorsement. Spoken lines keep the kill / clinical-trials / supplement / label hedges; the full "treatment of the premises" sentence is on the card.
